intro: In September 1615 Sir Thomas Roe came ashore at Surat as James I's ambassador to the Mughal emperor Jahangir, with a treaty to win for the East India Company and a cargo of presents he already feared were too poor. He reached the court at Ajmer at the end of December and was received on 10 January 1616 (Old Style). For the next three years he followed the moving court, south to the hill-fortress of Mandu in 1617 and west to Ahmedabad in 1618, and he wrote everything down.

The court he followed was also a studio. Jahangir had grown up in his father Akbar's painting workshops and kept the finest painters in Asia: Abu'l Hasan, Mansur, the young Bichitr, and the portraitist Bishandas, who spent these same years at the Persian court taking the likeness of Shah Abbas. The English gifts, the coach, the virginals, the portraits of the royal family, a miniature in Roe's pocket and a picture of Venus with a satyr, went straight into that world of looking, copying and judging. The court's craftsmen copied the coach. The painters copied the miniature so well that Roe could not find his own by candlelight. The English king's face turned up in a Mughal allegory, waiting at the foot of Jahangir's throne.

The record is not a set of diaries in the strict sense. Roe kept a journal and a letter-book, and Coryate wrote dated letters that were printed in London within two years. Jahangir wrote a memoir in Persian, arranged by regnal year and dated by day, which was meant to be read at court as his own portrait. Terry wrote his book long afterwards. The painters left no words except signatures and inscriptions, so they are heard through their pictures and through their patron. Nur Jahan, Asaf Khan and Prince Khurram appear only in what others wrote about them, and their entries are labelled that way.

Each of these sources has a point of view, and the chapter keeps them side by side rather than choosing between them. Roe is clever and often condescending; he sees obstruction where the court saw protocol, and insult where there may only have been curiosity. Jahangir records what he wished remembered and never once names the English ambassador who sat in his hall for three years. Where the two records meet, as on the November days in 1616 when the prince rode out in a copied English coach and the emperor left Ajmer in a European carriage, they agree almost to the day while describing quite different events.

A short prologue gives William Hawkins, the first Englishman to talk with Jahangir (1609–11), and a Persian counterpoint gives Pietro della Valle, a European writing about Shah Abbas's court in the years when Bishandas was painting it.

intro: On 6 May 1889 President Sadi Carnot opened the Exposition Universelle in Paris, a hundred years after the Estates-General met at Versailles. The fair filled the Champ de Mars, the Trocadéro across the Seine and the Esplanade des Invalides. Its gate was a 300-metre iron tower that Gustave Eiffel's firm had finished on 31 March. Over the next six months the Exposition had about thirty million visits before it closed on 31 October. Some of the strongest impressions it left were not in the official galleries. They were in a Javanese village, a café full of rejected painters, a Russian concert hall and a cowboy arena just outside the gates.

This chapter follows the fair through the people who left a dated record of it. Most of that record is letters and published writing rather than diaries. Edmond de Goncourt kept the one true journal, and he dined on the tower in July. The van Gogh family wrote letters between Paris and the asylum at Saint-Rémy. Gauguin wrote letters and a newspaper article from Brittany. The musicologist Julien Tiersot published his notes on the music within the year. Debussy's famous encounter with the gamelan, on the other hand, is known only from what he and a friend wrote years later, and it is marked that way here.

The tower itself had begun as a quarrel. In February 1887 writers and artists, Maupassant and Gounod among them, signed a protest in Le Temps against it, and Eiffel answered in the same paper. By September 1889 Gounod was lunching on the first platform with Eiffel and Thomas Edison, and Edison was writing Eiffel a dedication in praise of engineering. The Galerie des Machines beside it held Edison's phonographs. Elsewhere on the grounds, much less noticed, stood a Benz motor car.

The fair also put living people on show. About sixty Javanese and Sundanese lived in a kampong built for the Dutch section, and they danced and played the gamelan every day. On the Esplanade des Invalides the French Ministry of the Colonies built villages for people from New Caledonia, Senegal, the Sudan, Gabon and Indochina. Outside the gates, Buffalo Bill's Wild West brought about a hundred Lakota performers to Neuilly. These people appear almost entirely in other people's records: newspapers, engravings, photographs and the notes of visitors. The chapter says so plainly. It gives the few names that survive, such as the dancers Wakiem, Sariem, Soekia and Taminah and the Lakota leader Red Shirt, and it reports what was printed about them without repeating the visitors' gaze.

Read side by side, the eyes show one fair seen in very different ways. To Eiffel it was a triumph of building, and Maupassant fled from it. Theo van Gogh found its pictures weak. Rimsky-Korsakov played to thin houses. Debussy heard in the kampong a music that he said later made Western harmony look like a ghost. The people in the villages went home by train and steamer, and only a Javanese court record made forty years later tells something of the journey in their own language.

intro: In January 1897 the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, was observing Igue, the festival of the king's renewal, during which the Oba could receive no strangers. The British acting Consul-General of the Niger Coast Protectorate, James Phillips, set out to visit the Oba anyway. He wanted to open trade on the rivers and had asked London's leave to depose the king. The Oba's messengers asked him to wait. On 4 January, on the forest road from Gwato, Benin soldiers attacked the party; Phillips and most of his officers were killed with many of their carriers, and two officers escaped.

Within five weeks a naval force under Rear-Admiral Rawson had landed. It took Benin City on 18 February 1897, and three days later fire destroyed much of the city and the palace. From the palace the force removed thousands of objects: several hundred cast brass plaques that had lined its pillars, commemorative heads of past kings with carved tusks set into them, ivories, coral regalia and wooden figures. The officers' accounts described the city through its sacrifices and called it the City of Blood. Those descriptions were offered as the justification for the conquest; how accurate they were, and how far they reflected emergency rites in a city under attack, is still argued.

This chapter follows the objects from the palace to the sale room and the museum, and the king from the forest to the court and into exile. The record is uneven. On the British side there are a surgeon's diary, a survivor's book, despatches, a sailor's letter and the museum and dealers' registers. No writing by Oba Ovonramwen survives. His words reach us through messages reported by British officers and through the British court record of his trial. The Edo account was written down a generation later by Jacob Egharevba from the palace's own tradition. The chapter sets these out as positions and marks the later testimony as later.

The surprise in Europe was real and revealing. Curators trained on Renaissance metalwork found casting they compared to Cellini's, and at first credited it to Portuguese teachers; within a few years Luschan in Berlin and Ling Roth in Halifax were arguing that it was African. Webster's priced catalogues show how quickly the works became stock. The sale funded the expedition's costs and scattered the palace's collection across museums in Britain, Germany and the United States. A short coda notes the returns that began in the 2020s, as positions rather than a verdict.

Violence here is reported soberly. The killings of January and February are given in outline, and the expedition's claims about human sacrifice are reported as claims, without their detail. The record is mostly letters, logs, despatches, catalogues and published accounts rather than private diaries, and each eye is tagged accordingly.

title: The Gitanjali Year: Calcutta, London, Stockholm, 1912–1913
eyes: May Sinclair (Mary Amelia St Clair Sinclair)
Swedish Academy and its Nobel Committee (minutes, ballots and ceremony record)

places: London (Woburn Buildings); Normandy in late summer 1912

Shilaida on the Padma; London (Hampstead, then South Kensington); Urbana and Chi
Shilaida, on the Padma (now Kushtia, Bangladesh)

intro: In the spring of 1912 Rabindranath Tagore was fifty-one, the most famous poet in Bengal and almost unknown outside it. Illness had stopped him sailing for England in March. While he recovered on the family estate at Shilaida, on the Padma, he began writing out English prose versions of songs from his Bengali Gitanjali (1910) and other recent books in an exercise book. He did not, by his own account, expect much to come of it. Eighteen months later the Swedish Academy gave him the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first time it had gone to a writer from outside Europe.

This chapter follows the book between those two points: a notebook nearly lost on the London Underground, a painter's drawing room in Hampstead where Yeats read the poems aloud on 7 July 1912, a limited edition of 750 copies in cream silk, six poems in a three-month-old Chicago magazine, lectures to a Unitarian congregation in Urbana, Illinois, a trade edition from Macmillan, and a committee in Stockholm that could not read the original language and did not want to give him the prize. The full Academy overruled the committee on 13 November 1913. The next afternoon, at his school at Santiniketan, Tagore put a telegram in his pocket and did not open it.

The record is mostly letters, published articles, committee papers and memoirs written later, with very few diaries. The most immediate eyewitness accounts are C. F. Andrews's report of the Hampstead evening, printed in Calcutta a month later, and Edward Thompson's account of the two days at Santiniketan, written on 17 November 1913. Rothenstein's Men and Memories (1932) and Rathindranath Tagore's On the Edges of Time (1958) supply much of the familiar story but were written decades afterwards, and they are flagged. Tagore's Bengali letters are paraphrased. English texts printed before 1929, such as Yeats's introduction, Pound's notes and the newspapers, supply the few short quotations.

Laid side by side, these eyes show how a book was made by more than one person. Tagore translated, Rothenstein circulated, Yeats selected, reordered and introduced, and the India Society's officers changed words that both poets then fought over. Whether the English Gitanjali is Tagore's book, Yeats's or both is still argued, and the chapter reports the positions. The same pages show the reception moving outward, from the drawing room to Calcutta, Chicago, Stockholm and finally the press, which mixed delight with open racial contempt.

The chapter ends with a deputation from Calcutta. A trainload of notables came to Santiniketan to congratulate the poet whose Bengali work many of them had disparaged, and Tagore told them he could not accept their praise. Five days earlier he had written to Rothenstein that fame had been tied to him like a tin can to a dog's tail.

intro: In October 1921 José Vasconcelos took charge of Mexico's new Secretaría de Educación Pública. The country was coming out of a decade of revolution, and he set out to teach it to read and to give it pictures. He gave painters public walls, a small daily wage and themes. At the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria, the old Jesuit college of San Ildefonso, Diego Rivera began an encaustic allegory, 'La Creación', in the Anfiteatro Bolívar in 1922. Within months younger painters were working on the stairs and in the courtyards. Jean Charlot, a young Frenchman, completed one of the first true frescoes of the movement there between October 1922 and January 1923. José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros followed in 1923.

The painters organised. Their Syndicate of Technical Workers, Painters and Sculptors issued a manifesto on 9 December 1923, written by Siqueiros, that set public, monumental art against easel painting for private collectors. In 1924 the Syndicate began a newspaper, El Machete. That summer students of the Preparatoria scratched and damaged the frescoes by Orozco and Siqueiros. Vasconcelos resigned in July, his successor cut the budgets, and only Rivera, at the Ministry building, kept a large wall. He painted more than a hundred panels there between 1923 and 1928.

The second half of the chapter follows the walls north. Orozco painted 'Prometheus' at Pomona College in California in 1930 and 'The Epic of American Civilization' at Dartmouth from 1932 to 1934. Rivera painted the 'Detroit Industry' frescoes for the Detroit Institute of Arts between July 1932 and March 1933, paid for by Edsel Ford, and then went to New York to paint 'Man at the Crossroads' in the lobby of the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center. Each of these walls was argued over in public. In Detroit, clergy and a newspaper attacked the frescoes, and the museum's director, Edsel Ford and the architect Albert Kahn defended them. At Rockefeller Center the argument turned on the head of Lenin. Rivera added it in late April 1933, and on 4 May Nelson Rockefeller asked him in writing to replace it. Rivera refused, and work was stopped on 9 May. The mural was destroyed in February 1934. That same week Orozco signed the last of his Dartmouth panels, and later that year Rivera repainted the New York design in Mexico City's Palacio de Bellas Artes.

The record is mostly letters, dated inscriptions on the walls themselves, newspaper reports and diaries that were published long afterwards. Edward Weston's Mexican Daybooks appeared in 1961, Anita Brenner's journals in 2010, and Jean Charlot's shorthand diaries are still only partly decoded. Several principal witnesses wrote their memoirs years later: Vasconcelos (1935–39 and a short account for Charlot in 1945), Orozco (1945), Rivera (as told to Gladys March, 1960) and Siqueiros (1977). These are tagged as memoirs and used cautiously. Lucienne Bloch's diary of 1932–33 is known through the passages quoted by biographers and museum catalogues.

On the political quarrels the chapter reports positions. The painters argued that public walls belonged to the public and that the art could not be separated from its politics. Their critics in Mexico City, Detroit and New York argued that a school, a museum or a private office building owed nothing to a painter's politics, or that the work was ugly, foreign or offensive. The patrons held a third view: Edsel Ford and Valentiner stood by their walls, and the Rockefellers, who had commissioned theirs, stopped it and paid the painter in full.

intro: In the spring of 1935 the most famous actor in China played to Soviet audiences for about a month. Mei Lanfang (Mei Lan-fang in the older romanisation, 1894–1961) was a dan, a male performer of women's roles in jingju, the theatre Western audiences called Peking opera. He travelled at the invitation of VOKS, the All-Union Society for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries. His company of about two dozen performers and musicians sailed from Shanghai in late February on a Soviet steamer and crossed Siberia by the Far Eastern Express. They reached Moscow on 12 March, played there and in Leningrad, and gave a farewell performance at the Bolshoi on 13 April. On 14 April VOKS held a closed discussion of what the visit had shown. The directors Vsevolod Meyerhold and Alexander Tairov, the film-maker Sergei Eisenstein and the writer Sergei Tretyakov were among the people in Moscow that spring who wrote and spoke about him. Konstantin Stanislavsky, the most famous of them, stayed away from the public events. So were two foreigners, Edward Gordon Craig and Bertolt Brecht.

The prologue is the American tour of 1930. Mei's advisers, the dramatist Qi Rushan (Ch'i Ju-shan) and the Nankai University theatre man Zhang Pengchun (Chang P'eng-ch'un, known in English as P. C. Chang), had spent years preparing it. They cut the plays to Western lengths, wrote English programmes and had illustrations of hand gestures and costumes drawn. The company opened on Broadway at the 49th Street Theatre on 17 February 1930 and moved to the larger National Theatre in March. It then played Chicago, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Honolulu. In Los Angeles Mei met Charlie Chaplin, and the University of Southern California and Pomona College gave him honorary doctorates. Eisenstein, who was in Hollywood that summer, later wrote that he first heard of Mei from Chaplin.

The record is not a set of diaries. It is press articles dated by their issues (Tretyakov's pieces in Pravda, Eisenstein's in Komsomolskaya Pravda, the Shanghai and Tianjin dailies), programme essays, one letter (Marianne Moore's), the dated notebooks Craig called daybooks, the minutes of the 14 April meeting, and recollections that Mei and his deputy director Yu Shangyuan wrote down years later. The chapter tags each source by its form. The memoirs are marked as written later, because some of their best-known stories, above all Stanislavsky's praise, cannot be matched to anything written in 1935.

Two later inventions grew around the meeting of 14 April. In 1986 the Swedish Slavist Lars Kleberg staged a play in Kraków that imagined the discussion, with Brecht and Craig among the speakers. A French production directed by Antoine Vitez followed at Avignon in 1988 as 'Les Apprentis sorciers'. A Chinese translation then circulated in 1988 as if it were a record of what had been said. Kleberg later found the real stenographic minutes in the former Central State Archive of the October Revolution and published them in Russian in Iskusstvo kino (1992). A Chinese version appeared in Zhonghua xiqu in 1993. Secondary accounts of those minutes say that Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko chaired and that Tretyakov, Meyerhold and Eisenstein were among about thirty people who spoke or took part. They do not record Brecht or Erwin Piscator as speakers. Stanislavsky was not there. Accounts differ on Craig: his daybook has an entry for 14 April, but one Chinese account says the foreign guests were not on the invitation list. The chapter reports these positions without settling them. It does not quote the minutes.

The visit was also diplomacy. China and the Soviet Union had restored relations in December 1932, and the Chinese ambassador Yan Huiqing (W. W. Yen) travelled on the same ship. So did the film star Hu Die (Hu Tieh), on her way to the Moscow film festival. The Foreign Commissariat approved the speeches. The visit came three months after the murder of Kirov and as the doctrine of socialist realism was being pressed on the theatres. Soviet critics argued over whether Mei's conventions were a lesson in realism or a defence of the 'formalism' that Meyerhold was accused of. Within five years several of the hosts were dead. VOKS's chairman Alexander Arosev, Karl Radek, who had written on Mei in Izvestia, and Tretyakov were arrested in 1937. Tretyakov was killed that year and Arosev in 1938. Meyerhold was arrested in June 1939 and shot on 2 February 1940. The chapter records these deaths as a coda and does not read them back into what was written in 1935.
